# Model Context Protocol

[![MCP Logo](/modelcontextprotocol/.github/raw/main/profile/assets/light.png)](/modelcontextprotocol/.github/blob/main/profile/assets/light.png)

**A protocol for seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources**

[Documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) | [Specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) | [Discussions](https://github.com/orgs/modelcontextprotocol/discussions)

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol that enables seamless integration between LLM applications and external data sources and tools. Whether you're building an AI-powered IDE, enhancing a chat interface, or creating custom AI workflows, MCP provides a standardized way to connect LLMs with the context they need.

## Getting Started

* 📚 Read the [Documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) for guides and tutorials
* 🔍 Review the [Specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/latest) for protocol details
* 💻 Use our SDKs to start building:
  + [TypeScript SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk)
  + [Python SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk)
  + [Java SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/java-sdk)
  + [Kotlin SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/kotlin-sdk)
  + [C# SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/csharp-sdk)

  + [PHP SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/php-sdk)
  + [Ruby SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ruby-sdk)
  + [Rust SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/rust-sdk)
  + [Swift SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/swift-sdk)

## Project Structure

* [modelcontextprotocol](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol) - User documentation and protocol specification
* [typescript-sdk](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk) - TypeScript implementation
* [python-sdk](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk) - Python implementation
* [java-sdk](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/java-sdk) - Java implementation

* [create-kotlin-server](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/kotlin-sdk/tree/main/samples/kotlin-mcp-server) - Kotlin sample server
* [servers](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers) - List of maintained servers
* [ext-auth](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-auth) - List of authorization extensions

## Contributing

We welcome contributions of all kinds! Whether you want to fix bugs, improve documentation, or propose new features, please see our [contributing guide](/modelcontextprotocol/.github/blob/main/profile/CONTRIBUTING.md) to get started.

Have questions? Join the discussion in our [community forum](https://github.com/orgs/modelcontextprotocol/discussions).

## About

The Model Context Protocol is an open source project hosted by [The Linux Foundation](https://lfprojects.org) and open to contributions from the entire community.

URL: https://codelabs.developers.google.com/intro-a2a-purchasing-concierge

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Google Codelab tutorial on getting started with the Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol, specifically building a Purchasing Concierge agent that communicates with remote seller agents (Burger and Pizza) deployed on Cloud Run and Agent Engine. The A2A protocol standardizes communication between AI agents, complementing MCP (Model Context Protocol). While MCP focuses on connecting agents with tools and data, A2A enables agents to collaborate as agents rather than as tools.

The tutorial walks through deploying two A2A Server agents (Burger agent using CrewAI framework, Pizza agent using Langgraph framework) to Cloud Run, then deploying a Purchasing Concierge A2A Client agent (using ADK framework) to Vertex AI Agent Engine. Users interact with the concierge via a Gradio web UI to place orders with both seller agents.

Key technical concepts covered include:
- **Agent Card**: Published at `/.well-known/agent.json`, containing agent capabilities, skills, protocol version, supported modalities, and URL
- **A2A Flow**: Client discovers agent cards, sends messages (perceived as Tasks), server processes and returns artifacts
- **Core Objects**: Message, Task, Artifact, and Part
- **Agent Executor**: Handles incoming task execution and cancellation
- **Agent Engine**: Deploys ADK agents directly from Python scripts without custom backend services

The tutorial demonstrates that A2A allows agents built with completely different frameworks (CrewAI, Langgraph, ADK) to communicate seamlessly without sharing internal code or requiring the same language/deployment environment.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Announcing the Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) ---
URL: https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On April 9, 2025, Google announced the launch of the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, an open protocol designed to enable AI agents to communicate, securely exchange information, and coordinate actions across different enterprise platforms, frameworks, and vendors. The protocol is supported by over 50 technology partners including Atlassian, Box, Cohere, Intuit, LangChain, MongoDB, PayPal, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, UKG, and Workday, as well as leading service providers such as Accenture, BCG, Capgemini, Deloitte, HCLTech, Infosys, KPMG, McKinsey, PwC, TCS, and Wipro.

A2A is designed to complement Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) and follows five key design principles: embracing agentic capabilities (enabling agents to collaborate in unstructured modalities without sharing memory, tools, or context), building on existing standards (HTTP, SSE, JSON-RPC), being secure by default (supporting enterprise-grade authentication), supporting long-running tasks (from quick tasks to hours-long deep research), and being modality agnostic (supporting text, audio, and video streaming).

The protocol facilitates communication between a "client" agent and a "remote" agent through four key capabilities: capability discovery (using an "Agent Card" in JSON format), task management (oriented towards task completion with a defined lifecycle and state updates), collaboration (agents sending messages with context, replies, artifacts, or instructions), and user experience negotiation (each message includes "parts" with specified content types for format negotiation).

A real-world example demonstrated uses A2A for hiring: a hiring manager tasks an agent to find candidates matching a job listing, the agent interacts with specialized agents to source candidates, and after interviews, another agent facilitates background checks.

The protocol is released as open source with a full specification draft available on GitHub. Google is working with partners to launch a production-ready version later in 2025.
</summary>

URL: https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/agent2agent-protocol

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol is an open communication protocol for AI agents, initially introduced by Google in April 2025 and now housed by the Linux Foundation as an open-source project. It enables interoperability between AI agents from different providers or built with different frameworks, acting as a "universal translator" for agent ecosystems to break down silos.

**Key difference from MCP:** While the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI applications communicate with external services (APIs, databases, tools), A2A focuses specifically on agent-to-agent collaboration. The two protocols are complementary.

**Core architectural components:**
- A2A client (client agent) - initiates communication
- A2A server (remote agent) - processes tasks and responds
- Agent card - JSON file with agent metadata, capabilities, and authentication requirements
- Task - unit of work with a lifecycle (submitted, working, input-required, completed, failed)
- Message - fundamental communication unit with roles (user or agent)
- Artifact - tangible output (documents, images, etc.)
- Part - content piece within messages or artifacts (TextPart, FilePart, DataPart)

**How A2A works (3-step workflow):**
1. **Discovery** - Client agent finds remote agents and fetches their agent cards
2. **Authentication** - Based on security scheme in agent card (API keys, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect)
3. **Communication** - Tasks sent via HTTPS using JSON-RPC 2.0; supports long-running tasks with async webhooks, and real-time streaming via SSE

**Benefits:** Privacy (agents collaborate without revealing inner workings), seamless integration (built on HTTP, JSON-RPC, SSE), and enterprise-grade security.

**Status:** Early-stage protocol with planned improvements including formal authorization schemes, dynamic skill checking, UX negotiation, and enhanced streaming reliability.
</summary>

This article from Anthropic's engineering blog (published Nov 4, 2025) discusses how code execution with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can make AI agents more efficient by reducing token consumption. MCP is an open standard for connecting AI agents to external systems, and since its launch in November 2024, thousands of MCP servers have been built by the community.

The article identifies two key problems with scaling MCP usage:
1. **Tool definitions overload the context window** — Loading all tool definitions upfront (especially when connected to hundreds or thousands of tools) consumes hundreds of thousands of tokens before the agent even processes a request.
2. **Intermediate tool results consume additional tokens** — Large data (e.g., full meeting transcripts) must pass through the model's context multiple times during multi-step workflows.

The solution: Present MCP servers as code APIs rather than direct tool calls. The agent writes code to interact with MCP servers, allowing it to load only the tools it needs (reducing token usage from ~150,000 to ~2,000 tokens — a 98.7% savings) and process/filter data in the execution environment before passing results back to the model.

**Benefits include:**
- **Progressive disclosure** — Models navigate a filesystem of tools and load only what they need.
- **Context-efficient tool results** — Data can be filtered, aggregated, or transformed in code before the model sees it (e.g., showing 5 rows instead of 10,000).
- **More powerful control flow** — Loops, conditionals, and error handling use familiar code patterns rather than chained tool calls.
- **Privacy-preserving operations** — Intermediate results stay in the execution environment; PII can be tokenized before reaching the model.
- **State persistence and skills** — Agents can save intermediate results and reusable functions as "skills" for future use.

The article notes that code execution adds complexity, requiring secure sandboxing, resource limits, and monitoring. The benefits (reduced token costs, lower latency, improved tool composition) should be weighed against these implementation costs.
</summary>

<summary>
# Agent Protocols: A Complete Guide to MCP, A2A, and ACP

The article provides a comprehensive technical guide to the emerging agent communication protocol landscape as of 2026, which has consolidated under the Linux Foundation. The key development is the convergence of three competing standards into two complementary protocols:

**Consolidation Event (August 2025):** IBM's Agent Communication Protocol (ACP) joined forces with Google's Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) under the Linux Foundation's LF AI & Data umbrella. ACP development is winding down, with its stateful, asynchronous concepts being contributed directly to A2A v1.0.

## The Two Protocols

### Model Context Protocol (MCP)
- **Purpose:** Standardizes model-to-tool communication — how AI applications connect to data sources, tools, and workflows
- **Described as:** "A USB-C port for AI applications"
- **Technical basis:** JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio (local subprocess) or Streamable HTTP (remote)
- **State model:** Session-stateful with initialize/initialized handshake
- **Discovery:** Dynamic, in-session (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list after handshake)
- **Auth:** OAuth 2.1 flows for remote servers defined in MCP Authorization spec

### Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) v1.0
- **Purpose:** Standardizes agent-to-agent collaboration and task delegation across organizations
- **Technical basis:** JSON-RPC 2.0 (primary), gRPC, HTTP+JSON/REST bindings
- **State model:** Task-stateful with explicit state machine (SUBMITTED → WORKING → COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELED/REJECTED/INPUT_REQUIRED/AUTH_REQUIRED)
- **Discovery:** Static well-known URI (/.well-known/agent-card.json per RFC 8615) plus curated registries
- **Auth:** AgentCard.securitySchemes supporting API Key, OAuth 2.0, OIDC, mTLS
- **Agent Card:** Declares name, version, supportedInterfaces, capabilities, skills, and security schemes; SHOULD be signed using JWS (RFC 7515) over JCS-canonicalized card

## Recommended Architecture
The protocols are complementary, not competing. The recommended pattern is layered:
- **A2A** for high-level orchestration and inter-agent coordination
- **MCP** for low-level tool execution within specialist agents

## Security Considerations
Key threats include tool poisoning (MCP), Agent Card poisoning (A2A), prompt injection, excessive agency, and webhook spoofing/SSRF. Mitigations include signed Agent Cards, skill-scoped OAuth, MCP Authorization for remote servers, mTLS/DPoP, and LLM firewalls.

## Production Requirements
An API gateway is critical for centralized authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and observability. Recommended monitoring includes OpenTelemetry with W3C Trace Context, tracking Task state machine transitions, and logging taskId/contextId/authenticated identity.
</summary>

**Key Points:**

- **What A2A Is:** An open standard for communication between independent AI agent systems built on different frameworks. It handles agent discovery (via Agent Cards), task delegation, message exchange, streaming updates, and artifact sharing. It focuses on the full task lifecycle — not just function calls.

- **A2A vs MCP:** MCP (Model Context Protocol, from Anthropic) connects agents to tools. A2A connects agents to other agents. The cleanest architecture is layered: MCP for tool integration (below), A2A for agent collaboration (above). They are complementary, not competing.

- **Adoption Status (2026):** The Linux Foundation reports 150+ supporting organizations, major cloud platform integrations, and production deployments across multiple industries. A2A has crossed from "Google announcement" to a formal specification with governance momentum and ecosystem growth.

- **Where A2A Is Useful:** Independently deployed agents owned by different teams, built with different frameworks, with their own tools/permissions, handling long-running tasks, and operating across organizational boundaries. Example: an enterprise assistant delegating to procurement, legal, finance, compliance, and market research agents.

- **Where A2A Is Overhyped:** Most projects don't need it — local coding assistants, chatbots, small internal automation, or single-workflow systems. It's unnecessary when there's only one agent, all components share one codebase, workflows are short/synchronous, or an API or queue would suffice.

- **Decision Framework:** No A2A for local workflows. MCP for tool access. A2A for agent peers. Both for layered architectures.

- **Final Verdict:** A2A is not dead, not universal, and not the protocol most developers should start with (MCP comes first). But for multi-agent enterprise systems with real deployment and ownership boundaries, A2A is worth serious attention.

--- SOURCE 5: Code execution with MCP: building more efficient AI agents ---
URL: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Anthropic's engineering blog (published Nov 4, 2025) discusses how code execution with the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can make AI agents more efficient by reducing token consumption. MCP is an open standard for connecting AI agents to external systems, and since its launch in November 2024, thousands of MCP servers have been built by the community.

The article identifies two key problems with scaling MCP usage:
1. **Tool definitions overload the context window** — Loading all tool definitions upfront (especially when connected to hundreds or thousands of tools) consumes hundreds of thousands of tokens before the agent even processes a request.
2. **Intermediate tool results consume additional tokens** — Large data (e.g., full meeting transcripts) must pass through the model's context multiple times during multi-step workflows.

The solution: Present MCP servers as code APIs rather than direct tool calls. The agent writes code to interact with MCP servers, allowing it to load only the tools it needs (reducing token usage from ~150,000 to ~2,000 tokens — a 98.7% savings) and process/filter data in the execution environment before passing results back to the model.

**Benefits include:**
- **Progressive disclosure** — Models navigate a filesystem of tools and load only what they need.
- **Context-efficient tool results** — Data can be filtered, aggregated, or transformed in code before the model sees it (e.g., showing 5 rows instead of 10,000).
- **More powerful control flow** — Loops, conditionals, and error handling use familiar code patterns rather than chained tool calls.
- **Privacy-preserving operations** — Intermediate results stay in the execution environment; PII can be tokenized before reaching the model.
- **State persistence and skills** — Agents can save intermediate results and reusable functions as "skills" for future use.

The article notes that code execution adds complexity, requiring secure sandboxing, resource limits, and monitoring. The benefits (reduced token costs, lower latency, improved tool composition) should be weighed against these implementation costs.
</summary>

URL: https://tyk.io/learning-center/agent-protocols-a-complete-guide-to-mcp-a2a-and-acp

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Agent Protocols: A Complete Guide to MCP, A2A, and ACP

The article provides a comprehensive technical guide to the emerging agent communication protocol landscape as of 2026, which has consolidated under the Linux Foundation. The key development is the convergence of three competing standards into two complementary protocols:

**Consolidation Event (August 2025):** IBM's Agent Communication Protocol (ACP) joined forces with Google's Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) under the Linux Foundation's LF AI & Data umbrella. ACP development is winding down, with its stateful, asynchronous concepts being contributed directly to A2A v1.0.

## The Two Protocols

### Model Context Protocol (MCP)
- **Purpose:** Standardizes model-to-tool communication — how AI applications connect to data sources, tools, and workflows
- **Described as:** "A USB-C port for AI applications"
- **Technical basis:** JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio (local subprocess) or Streamable HTTP (remote)
- **State model:** Session-stateful with initialize/initialized handshake
- **Discovery:** Dynamic, in-session (tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list after handshake)
- **Auth:** OAuth 2.1 flows for remote servers defined in MCP Authorization spec

### Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A) v1.0
- **Purpose:** Standardizes agent-to-agent collaboration and task delegation across organizations
- **Technical basis:** JSON-RPC 2.0 (primary), gRPC, HTTP+JSON/REST bindings
- **State model:** Task-stateful with explicit state machine (SUBMITTED → WORKING → COMPLETED/FAILED/CANCELED/REJECTED/INPUT_REQUIRED/AUTH_REQUIRED)
- **Discovery:** Static well-known URI (/.well-known/agent-card.json per RFC 8615) plus curated registries
- **Auth:** AgentCard.securitySchemes supporting API Key, OAuth 2.0, OIDC, mTLS
- **Agent Card:** Declares name, version, supportedInterfaces, capabilities, skills, and security schemes; SHOULD be signed using JWS (RFC 7515) over JCS-canonicalized card

## Recommended Architecture
The protocols are complementary, not competing. The recommended pattern is layered:
- **A2A** for high-level orchestration and inter-agent coordination
- **MCP** for low-level tool execution within specialist agents

## Security Considerations
Key threats include tool poisoning (MCP), Agent Card poisoning (A2A), prompt injection, excessive agency, and webhook spoofing/SSRF. Mitigations include signed Agent Cards, skill-scoped OAuth, MCP Authorization for remote servers, mTLS/DPoP, and LLM firewalls.

## Production Requirements
An API gateway is critical for centralized authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and observability. Recommended monitoring includes OpenTelemetry with W3C Trace Context, tracking Task state machine transitions, and logging taskId/contextId/authenticated identity.

This article from Rost Glukhov's technical blog provides an updated assessment of Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol as of April 2026, one year after its announcement. It examines the protocol's adoption, practical use cases, and ongoing debates.

**Key Points:**

- **What A2A Is:** An open standard for communication between independent AI agent systems built on different frameworks. It handles agent discovery (via Agent Cards), task delegation, message exchange, streaming updates, and artifact sharing. It focuses on the full task lifecycle — not just function calls.

- **A2A vs MCP:** MCP (Model Context Protocol, from Anthropic) connects agents to tools. A2A connects agents to other agents. The cleanest architecture is layered: MCP for tool integration (below), A2A for agent collaboration (above). They are complementary, not competing.

- **Adoption Status (2026):** The Linux Foundation reports 150+ supporting organizations, major cloud platform integrations, and production deployments across multiple industries. A2A has crossed from "Google announcement" to a formal specification with governance momentum and ecosystem growth.

- **Where A2A Is Useful:** Independently deployed agents owned by different teams, built with different frameworks, with their own tools/permissions, handling long-running tasks, and operating across organizational boundaries. Example: an enterprise assistant delegating to procurement, legal, finance, compliance, and market research agents.

- **Where A2A Is Overhyped:** Most projects don't need it — local coding assistants, chatbots, small internal automation, or single-workflow systems. It's unnecessary when there's only one agent, all components share one codebase, workflows are short/synchronous, or an API or queue would suffice.

- **Security Challenges:** The biggest unresolved issues are trust problems — agent identity, authorization, audit trails, delegation tracking, artifact provenance, and observability across boundaries. A2A is a communication protocol, not a security architecture.

- **The Google Problem:** Skepticism persists due to Google's history of abandoning platforms, but Linux Foundation hosting has reduced that concern. A2A should be judged as an emerging interoperability standard, not just "Google's protocol."

- **Realistic Near-Term Use:** Internal enterprise agent networks (HR, finance, support, DevOps, security agents) rather than public agent marketplaces.

- **Decision Framework:** No A2A for local workflows. MCP for tool access. A2A for agent peers. Both for layered architectures.

- **Final Verdict:** A2A is not dead, not universal, and not the protocol most developers should start with (MCP comes first). But for multi-agent enterprise systems with real deployment and ownership boundaries, A2A is worth serious attention.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On August 17, 2026, Axios reported that the Google-backed Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A), a standard enabling AI agents to communicate with one another, is moving to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). This places A2A alongside the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with A2A handling agent-to-agent communication while MCP handles connections between AI apps and tools/data. AAIF has grown from fewer than 40 members to over 250 since its launch in December 2025, with backers including Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Anthropic, OpenAI, Bloomberg, Shopify, and Block. Google Cloud VP Rao Surapaneni noted the protocol addresses customer needs for interoperability between agentic systems from different providers. AAIF executive director Mazin Gilbert emphasized the move provides a neutral home for developing open standards for AI agent communication. The transition aims to push the industry toward more modular, model-agnostic AI systems, giving companies flexibility to choose providers based on cost, performance, or latency needs.
</summary>

When we first envisioned A2A, the hypothesis was customers are deploying agentic systems from multiple technology providers and platform providers, Google Cloud VP Rao Surapaneni told Axios, There's a big difference between an open protocol and open standard, and having an open protocol becoming interoperable with the entire stack, AAIF executive director Mazin Gilbert said in an interview. Welcome to the official code samples and demonstrations for the [Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol](https://goo.gle/a2a).

We are thrilled to have you here! Whether you are exploring multi-agent architectures for the first time or building advanced interoperable agent networks, this repository provides simple, inspiring, and accessible learning resources to accelerate your development.

## Why Agent2Agent?

In a world of diverse AI frameworks and ecosystems, agents need a common language to communicate, collaborate, and delegate tasks securely. The A2A protocol establishes a standardized, open standard for multi-agent interoperability.

Our samples demonstrate how easily complex multi-agent problems can be solved across different languages and host applications.

## Quick Start

Get up and running immediately by launching a Helloworld agent and communicating with it via our Python CLI host.

1. **Start the Agent Server**: Open a terminal, navigate to the Helloworld agent directory, set up a virtual environment, install the dependencies, and start the server:

   ```
   cd source
   ```
2. **Run the Host Client**: Open a second terminal, navigate to the Helloworld agent directory, activate the virtual environment, and run the test client:

   ```
   cd source
   ```

## Disclaimer

**Important:** The sample code provided is for demonstration purposes and illustrates the mechanics of the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. When building production applications, it is critical to treat any agent operating outside of your direct control as a potentially untrusted entity.

All data received from an external agent—including but not limited to its AgentCard, messages, artifacts, and task statuses—should be handled as untrusted input. For example, a malicious agent could provide an AgentCard containing crafted data in its fields (e.g., description, name, skills.description). If this data is used without sanitization to construct prompts for a Large Language Model (LLM), it could expose your application to prompt injection attacks. Failure to properly validate and sanitize this data before use can introduce security vulnerabilities into your application.

> Developers are responsible for implementing appropriate security measures, such as input validation and secure handling of credentials to protect their systems and users.

automatically visible in `/docs` (see [#280](https://github.com/a2aproject/a2a-python/pull/280)). The v1.0 rewrite dropped that wrapper in favour of bare Starlette route factories (`create_agent_card_routes`, `create_jsonrpc_routes`, `create_rest_routes`). These return `starlette.routing.Route` objects; FastAPI's OpenAPI generator only enumerates `fastapi.routing.APIRoute` instances, so every A2A endpoint silently vanished from `/docs` and `/openapi.json`. args.summary:
This is the GitHub repository page for **a2aproject/a2a-python**, a public Python SDK (version 1.1.3, released Aug 18, 2026) for the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol. The repository has 741 commits, 54 branches, 59 tags, 2.1k stars, and 482 forks. Key recent developments include:

- **v1.0 Migration (PR #572):** The SDK was upgraded from Pydantic-based types to protobuf-generated types per A2A v1.0 specs. Breaking changes include new `Role` enum values (`ROLE_USER`/`ROLE_AGENT`) and `TaskState` enum with `TASK_STATE_*` prefix. 601 tests pass.
- **FastAPI /docs Restoration (PR #1024):** A new helper function `add_a2a_routes_to_fastapi()` re-registers A2A Starlette routes as FastAPI `APIRoute` instances so they appear in Swagger UI `/docs` and `/openapi.json`. Includes rich request-body schemas from proto descriptors, proto `oneof` → JSON Schema `oneOf`, and pre-filled `A2A-Version: 1.0` header.
- **Swagger Example Annotations (PR #1092):** Improved Swagger example annotations in the proto → JSON Schema generator, driven by `google.api.field_behavior` annotations.
- **gRPC Rich Error Handling (PR #790):** Implemented standard gRPC rich error handling using `google.rpc.Status` and `google.rpc.ErrorInfo` via `grpc-status-details-bin`.
- **DefaultRequestHandlerV2 Fix (PR #1153):** Added a warning when `queue_manager` is passed to `DefaultRequestHandlerV2` but ignored (v2 uses in-memory `ActiveTaskRegistry` instead).
- **Agent Guidance (PR #1059):** Promoted `AGENTS.md` as the cross-agent source of truth, added a mistake-reflection workflow with `evidence_rules.md`.
- **CI/CD:** Uses release-please, itk nightly runs, and various CI improvements.

[gRPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#10-grpc-protocol-binding) - [HTTP](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#11-httpjsonrest-protocol-binding) - [JSON Examples](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#416-filepart) provided for protobuf definitions of data model objects that previously used discriminators - Clarification of returned errors where multiple are applicable. e.g. [Cancel Task](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#315-cancel-task) - (#1160) Related to #1151 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/998 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1091 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1072 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1058 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/975 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1105 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/989 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1189 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1187 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1177 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1180 Fixes https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A/issues/1172 In order to more effectively describe the A2A protocol in a consistent way across different protocols, this PR refactors the specification to describe the application protocol in a transport agnostic way, and then have separate sections that describe how each of the transports map to the abstract application protocol. To see a preview of what it looks like you can go here https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/ The goal of the TSC is to use the changes in this PR as the baseline for a v1.0 Release Candidate. This will give SDK maintainers an stable document to validate the changes in the specification through implementations before v1.0 release. There are many pending feature requests for the A2A specifications that the TSC are supportive of. However, getting a stable, consistent, unambiguous, multi-protocol specification is necessary before additional features can be added safely. ## Document Restructuring - [A2A Operations](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#3-a2a-protocol-operations) are described independent of wire protocol - [Protocol Data Model](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#4-protocol-data-model) is described using protobuf as source of truth. All other serializations are derived from that. - Protocol bindings (formerly described as transports) are now described in their own sections - [JSON-RPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#9-json-rpc-protocol-binding) - [gRPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#10-grpc-protocol-binding) - [HTTP](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#11-httpjsonrest-protocol-binding) - [Operation Parameters ](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#32-operation-parameter-objects) describe structures reused across different operations - [Operation Semantics](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#33-operation-semantics) describe common behavior patterns across operations ## New Sections - [Requirements Language](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#21-requirements-language) - [Capability Validation](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#334-capability-validation) - [Abstract description of error handling](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#332-error-handling) - [Abstract description of \"headers\"](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#325-headers) - [Extensions](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#46-extensions) - [Versioning](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#36-versioning) - [Custom Binding Guidelines](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#12-custom-binding-guidelines) - [JSON Field Naming Conventions](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#54-json-field-naming-convention) - [Data Type Conventions](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#55-data-type-conventions) - [Security Considerations](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#77-security-considerations) - [Agent Card Signing](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#84-agent-card-signing) - [IANA Considerations](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#13-iana-considerations) ## Protocol Clarifications - Defining order for events returned from [Stream Message](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#312-stream-message) - [JSON Examples](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#416-filepart) provided for protobuf definitions of data model objects that previously used discriminators - Clarification of returned errors where multiple are applicable. e.g. [Cancel Task](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#315-cancel-task) - Defined returned events and usage scenarios for [Resubscribe](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#316-resubscribe-to-task) - Defined protocol binding for errors using protocol native capabilities for all bindings - [JSON-RPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#94-error-handling) - [gRPC](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#104-error-handling) - [HTTP](https://purple-moss-0838db51e.3.azurestaticapps.net/specification/#115-error-handling) ## Artifact Generation The scripts have been changed to enable a2a.json to be generated from the a2a.proto so that a2a.proto and specification.md are the only normative source. Additional work is required to align the generated a2a.json with the original one. The webpage is the GitHub repository for the **Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol**, an open-source project under the `a2aproject` organization. The repository has 25.4k stars and 2.6k forks, with 613 commits as of the latest update on August 18, 2026. The A2A protocol enables inter-agent communication across different protocols.

Key recent developments include:
- A major refactor of the specification (PR #1160) to separate the application protocol definition from transport mappings, establishing a v1.0 Release Candidate baseline. The specification now describes A2A operations independently of wire protocol, uses protobuf as the source of truth for the data model, and defines separate protocol bindings for JSON-RPC, gRPC, and HTTP/JSON-REST.
- New sections added to the specification include: Requirements Language, Capability Validation, error handling, headers, Extensions, Versioning, Custom Binding Guidelines, JSON Field Naming Conventions, Data Type Conventions, Security Considerations, Agent Card Signing, and IANA Considerations.
- The repository is versioned at v1.0.1 (released April 23, 2026), with bug fixes related to HTTP binding content type and transcoding errors.
- SDK repositories are available for Python, Go, Java, JavaScript, .NET, and Rust.
- The project has a governance structure with a Technical Steering Committee (TSC) and is licensed under Apache 2.0.
- Changes include updates to governance documentation, security vulnerability intake moved to GitHub Security Advisories, and a daily docs link check workflow implemented.

# Blog

Tags: 

* Artificial Intelligence

## Mastering Google’s A2A Protocol: The Complete Guide to Agent-to-Agent Communication

Posted On: 20 November, 2025

![](/themes/custom/cybage/images/resource_center/Blog-card-image.webp)

This is Part 2 of our series on Building Intelligent AI Systems. In [Part 1](https://www.cybage.com/blog/building-intelligent-ai-systems-understanding-agentic-ai-and-design-patterns), we explored Agentic AI fundamentals and design patterns. Now, let’s dive deep into [Google’s Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability/) — the game-changing standard that’s revolutionizing how AI agents communicate and collaborate.

### **Introducing Google’s A2A Protocol**

The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol addresses a critical challenge in modern AI deployment: enabling seamless communication between agents developed on different platforms, frameworks, and cloud environments.

Image

![Diagram showing Google A2A Protocol interaction between Client Agent and Remote Agent, illustrating secure collaboration, task and state management, user experience negotiation, and capability discovery.](/sites/default/files/styles/large/public/2025-11/Visualization%20of%20Google%E2%80%99s%20A2A%20Protocol%20enabling%20communication%20between%20Client%20and%20Remote%20Agents%20for%20secure%20collaboration%2C%20task%20management%2C%20and%20capability%20discovery..webp?itok=OE_rySes)

Visualization of Google’s A2A Protocol enabling communication between Client and Remote Agents   
for secure collaboration, task management, and capability discovery.

### 

### **Key Features of A2A Protocol**

* **Standardized Communication:** Universal messaging format across all AI agents
* **Cross-Platform Compatibility:** Seamless integration regardless of underlying technology
* **Scalable Architecture:** Easily add new agents without system disruption
* **Real-time Collaboration:** Instant communication and task coordination
* **Enterprise-Ready:** Built-in security and authentication mechanisms

### 

### **What Makes A2A Essential**

A2A protocol serves as a universal communication standard that allows AI agents to:

* Share goals and coordinate tasks across platforms
* Exchange data and context in standardized formats
* Collaborate regardless of underlying technology stack
* Operate in distributed, cloud-agnostic environments

### 

### **The Interoperability Challenge**

Before A2A, organizations faced significant challenges:

* **Custom Integration Overhead**: Each agent connection required bespoke development
* **Inconsistent Communication**: Different formats across agent implementations
* **Limited Scalability**: Tightly coupled systems difficult to extend
* **Maintenance Complexity**: Multiple integration points to manage

A2A protocol transforms this landscape by providing:

* **Standardized Communication**: Consistent message formats across all agents
* **Plug-and-Play Integration**: Easy addition of new agents without system disruption
* **Cross-Platform Compatibility**: Seamless operation across different frameworks
* **Reduced Development Time**: Standard implementation patterns
* **Framework Agnostic:** A2A offers a standard interface regardless of the chosen agentic framework.

Image

![A2A Protocol enabling communication between a Client Agent and multiple Remote Agents, including Crewai and LangChain, for cross-platform AI collaboration.](/sites/default/files/2025-11/Google%E2%80%99s%20Agent-to-Agent%20%28A2A%29%20Protocol%20connecting%20Client%20Agents%20with%20Remote%20Agent%20coded%20using%20frameworks%20like%20Crewai%20and%20LangChain%20for%20seamless%20interoperability..webp)

Google’s Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol connecting Client Agents with Remote Agent coded using frameworks like Crewai and LangChain for seamless interoperability

### 

### **Core Components of A2A Protocol**

Understanding A2A implementation requires familiarity with its fundamental components:

Image

![Google A2A Protocol structure illustrating relationships between A2A Client, A2A Server, Agent Card, Task, Message, Push Notification, and Streaming components.](/sites/default/files/2025-11/Google%E2%80%99s%20Agent-to-Agent%20%28A2A%29%20Protocol%20showcasing%20core%20components%20such%20as%20A2A%20Client%2C%20Server%2C%20Task%20Management%2C%20Messaging%2C%20and%20Streaming..webp)

Google’s Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol showcasing core components such as A2A Client, Server, Task Management, Messaging, and Streaming.

#### **Agent Discovery**

* **Agent Card**: Metadata profile describing capabilities and communication preferences
* **Discovery Endpoint**: Standardized location for agent information (/.well-known/agent.json)
* **Capability Matching**: Automated selection of appropriate agents for specific tasks

#### **A2A Client & Server**

The A2A protocol operates through two main components:

* **A2A Client:** Initiates communication with remote agents, handles task submission, and monitors progress
* **A2A Server:** Receives and processes incoming tasks, manages agent capabilities, and returns results

#### **Task Management**

* **Task Object**: Structured work units with clear objectives and data
* **Status Tracking**: Real-time progress monitoring (pending, working, completed)
* **Artifact Handling**: Structured output containing results in multiple formats

#### **Communication Protocols**

* **Message Exchange**: Structured communication between agents
* **Push Notifications**: Real-time updates on task progress and status changes
* **Streaming Support**: Continuous data exchange for long-running tasks

### 

### **A2A Communication Flow Implementation**

The A2A protocol defines a four-step communication process ensuring consistency and reliability:

Image

![A2A communication process flowchart showing agent discovery, task initiation, status tracking, and result delivery.](/sites/default/files/2025-11/Step-by-step%20flow%20of%20A2A%20communication%20from%20agent%20discovery%20to%20result%20delivery._0.webp)

Step-by-step flow of A2A communication from agent discovery to result delivery.

Image

![Diagram of A2A communication flow showing step-by-step process — Agent Discovery, Task Initiation, Status Updates, and Result Delivery — used for structured agent interactions.](/sites/default/files/2025-11/Four-step%20A2A%20communication%20process%20demonstrating%20agent%20discovery%2C%20task%20initiation%2C%20status%20updates%2C%20and%20result%20delivery%20for%20seamless%20multi-agent%20coordination..webp)

Four-step A2A communication process demonstrating agent discovery, task initiation, status updates, and result delivery for seamless multi-agent coordination.

### **Code Examples for A2A Implementation**

#### **A2A Client Implementation**

import requests  
import json  
from typing import Dict, Any, Optional  
  
class A2AClient:  
def \_\_init\_\_(self, base\_url: str, auth\_token: Optional[str] = None):  
self.base\_url = base\_url  
self.auth\_token = auth\_token  
self.headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"}  
if auth\_token:  
self.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {auth\_token}"  
  
## Step 1 : Agent Discovery  
async def discover\_agent(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:  
"""Retrieve agent capabilities and endpoints"""  
url = f"{self.base\_url}/.well-known/agent.json"  
response = requests.get(url, headers=self.headers)  
response.raise\_for\_status()  
return response.json()  
  
## Step 2: Task Initiation  
async def send\_task(self, task\_data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:  
"""Send task to remote agent"""  
agent\_info = await self.discover\_agent()  
task\_endpoint = agent\_info["endpoints"]["tasks"]  
  
url = f"{self.base\_url}{task\_endpoint}"  
response = requests.post(url, json=task\_data, headers=self.headers)  
response.raise\_for\_status()  
return response.json()  
  
## Step 3 : Get Status Updates  
async def get\_task\_status(self, task\_id: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:  
"""Check task progress and status"""  
url = f"{self.base\_url}/api/tasks/{task\_id}/status"  
response = requests.get(url, headers=self.headers)  
response.raise\_for\_status()  
return response.json()  
  
## Step 4 : Process Request & Get Results  
async def process\_customer\_feedback():  
client = A2AClient("https://sentiment-agent.example.com", "your-auth-token")  
  
task\_data = {  
"task\_id": "feedback-analysis-001",  
"message": "Analyze customer sentiment",  
"parts": [  
{  
"type": "text",  
"content": "Customer feedback data to analyze..."  
}  
]  
}  
  
result = await client.send\_task(task\_data)  
print(f"Task submitted: {result['task\_id']}")  
  
# Monitor task progress  
while True:  
status = await client.get\_task\_status(result['task\_id'])  
if status['status'] == 'completed':  
print(f"Analysis complete: {status['artifacts']}")  
break  
elif status['status'] == 'failed':  
print(f"Task failed: {status['error']}")  
break

#### **A2A Server Implementation**

Python (Flask-based) Example:

from flask import Flask, request, jsonify  
import uuid  
from datetime import datetime  
from typing import Dict, Any  
  
app = Flask(\_\_name\_\_)  
  
class A2AServer:  
def \_\_init\_\_(self):  
self.tasks = {}  
self.agent\_capabilities = {  
"name": "Sentiment Analysis Agent",  
"version": "1.0.0",  
"capabilities": [  
"sentiment-analysis",  
"text-classification",  
"emotion-detection"  
],  
"endpoints": {  
"tasks": "/api/tasks/send",  
"status": "/api/tasks/{task\_id}/status"  
}  
}  
  
def process\_task(self, task\_data: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:  
"""Process incoming task and return result"""  
task\_id = task\_data.get('task\_id', str(uuid.uuid4()))  
  
# Simulate task processing  
self.tasks[task\_id] = {  
"status": "working",  
"created\_at": datetime.now().isoformat(),  
"progress": 0  
}  
  
# Actual processing logic would go here  
result = {  
"sentiment\_scores": {  
"positive": 0.75,  
"neutral": 0.15,  
"negative": 0.10  
},  
"confidence": 0.92  
}  
  
self.tasks[task\_id] = {  
"status": "completed",  
"artifacts": [{"type": "data", "content": result}],  
"completed\_at": datetime.now().isoformat()  
}  
  
return self.tasks[task\_id]  
  
server = A2AServer()  
  
@app.route('/.well-known/agent.json', methods=['GET'])  
def get\_agent\_card():  
"""Return agent capabilities and endpoints"""  
return jsonify(server.agent\_capabilities)  
  
@app.route('/api/tasks/send', methods=['POST'])  
def send\_task():  
"""Process incoming task request"""  
task\_data = request.json  
result = server.process\_task(task\_data)  
return jsonify(result)  
  
@app.route('/api/tasks//status', methods=['GET'])  
def get\_task\_status(task\_id):  
"""Return task status and progress"""  
if task\_id not in server.tasks:  
return jsonify({"error": "Task not found"}), 404  
  
return jsonify(server.tasks[task\_id])  
  
if \_\_name\_\_ == '\_\_main\_\_':  
app.run(debug=True, port=5000)

### 

#### **Streaming Task Execution**

For long-running processes, A2A supports streaming communication using   
tasks/sendSubscribe:

POST /api/tasks/sendSubscribe  
{  
"task\_id": "streaming-task-001",  
"message": "Generate comprehensive market analysis report",  
"stream": true  
}

**Streaming responses:**

## Intermediatory Task Status  
{  
"state": "working",  
"final": false,  
"partial\_result": "Completed market size analysis..."  
}  
## Status and final response once the task is completed  
{  
"state": "completed",  
"final": true,  
"artifacts": [  
{  
"report\_url": "https://results.example.com/report.pdf"  
}  
]  
}

### **UX Negotiation and Structured Data Exchange**

A2A also supports UX negotiation so that structured data exchange could take place. Following is one example showcasing UX negotiation for reimbursement form interaction:

#### **Example: Reimbursement Form Interaction**

Image

![User interface example of A2A form negotiation showing interactive data capture and validation.](/sites/default/files/2025-11/User%20interface%20example%20of%20A2A%20form%20negotiation%20showing%20interactive%20data%20capture%20and%20validation..webp)

AI agent-assisted form negotiation for structured data input using the A2A protocol.

Here’s real-world use case where an AI agent assists a user in submitting a reimbursement request.

* **Conversational Confirmation:**  
  The agent confirms the amount and asks for the purpose of the reimbursement through natural language prompts.
* **Structured Data Capture:**  
  A form is presented to the user to input:  
  – **Transaction Date:** e.g., 17–04–2025  
  – **Amount:** e.g., ₹2,50,000  
  – **Purpose:** e.g., Work Related, Item: Laptop  
  – **Request ID:** e.g., request\_id\_5150819
* **Actionable Interface:**  
  The user can review and submit the form, ensuring clarity and accuracy before the data is processed.

{  
"interaction\_type": "form\_negotiation",  
"fields": [  
{  
"name": "transaction\_date",  
"type": "date",  
"required": true  
},  
{  
"name": "amount",  
"type": "currency",  
"validation": "positive\_number"  
},  
{  
"name": "purpose",  
"type": "select",  
"options": ["Work Related", "Personal", "Training"]  
}  
]  
}

#### **Message Communication with Multiple A2A Compliant Agents**

The A2A Client Agent can communicate with multiple remote agents using A2A protocol for managing communication between multiple specialized agents:

Image

![A2A Host Agent diagram showing message communication across multiple specialized AI agents.](/sites/default/files/2025-11/A2A%20Host%20Agent%20diagram%20showing%20message%20communication%20across%20multiple%20specialized%20AI%20agents..webp)

Central A2A Host Agent managing multi-agent communication and orchestration.

### 

### **Integration with Model Context Protocol (MCP)**

A2A protocol works seamlessly with MCP to enable secure, multi-channel agent collaboration across enterprise systems. Following system diagram showcase how 2 agents interacts with each other and each agent independently can integrate with multiple MCP servers to complete a given task.

Image

Integration of A2A protocol with Model Context Protocol (MCP) for enterprise-wide AI collaboration.

### 

#### **Sample Code Example for Integration of A2A Protocol with MCP**

class A2AMCPIntegration:  
def \_\_init\_\_(self):  
self.mcp\_clients = {}  
self.a2a\_agents = {}  
  
async def setup\_enterprise\_integration(self):  
"""Configure MCP clients for enterprise systems"""  
self.mcp\_clients = {  
"google\_drive": MCPClient("google-drive-server"),  
"slack": MCPClient("slack-integration-server"),  
"database": MCPClient("enterprise-db-server")  
}  
  
async def process\_cross\_platform\_task(self, task\_data: Dict[str, Any]):  
"""Handle tasks requiring multiple systems"""  
# Use A2A to coordinate with AI agents  
analysis\_agent = A2AClient("https://analysis-agent.company.com")  
analysis\_result = await analysis\_agent.send\_task({  
"message": "Analyze quarterly reports",  
"parts": task\_data["input\_data"]  
})  
  
# Use MCP to interact with enterprise systems  
await self.mcp\_clients["google\_drive"].save\_file({  
"filename": "quarterly\_analysis.pdf",  
"content": analysis\_result["artifacts"][0]["content"]  
})  
  
await self.mcp\_clients["slack"].send\_notification({  
"channel": "#executive-reports",  
"message": "Quarterly analysis complete and saved to Google Drive"  
})  
  
return {  
"status": "completed",  
"analysis": analysis\_result,  
"file\_location": "Google Drive",  
"notifications\_sent": ["Slack"]  
}

This is Part 2 of Cybage's series on Building Intelligent AI Systems, providing a comprehensive guide to Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol. The A2A protocol addresses the critical challenge of enabling seamless communication between AI agents developed on different platforms, frameworks, and cloud environments.

**Key Features:** Standardized communication, cross-platform compatibility, scalable architecture, real-time collaboration, and enterprise-ready security.

**Before A2A:** Organizations faced custom integration overhead, inconsistent communication, limited scalability, and maintenance complexity.

**Core Components:**
- **Agent Discovery:** Agent Card (metadata profile), Discovery Endpoint (/.well-known/agent.json), Capability Matching
- **A2A Client & Server:** Client initiates communication/task submission, Server processes tasks and returns results
- **Task Management:** Structured work units, status tracking (pending/working/completed), artifact handling
- **Communication Protocols:** Message exchange, push notifications, streaming support

**Communication Flow:** Four-step process: 1) Agent Discovery, 2) Task Initiation, 3) Status Tracking, 4) Result Delivery

The guide includes Python code examples for A2A Client implementation (using requests and async/await patterns) and A2A Server implementation (Flask-based). It also covers streaming task execution via tasks/sendSubscribe, UX negotiation for structured data exchange (e.g., reimbursement form interaction), and integration with Model Context Protocol (MCP) for enterprise-wide AI collaboration.

**Multi-Agent Architecture:** The protocol enables a host agent to orchestrate communication between specialized agents (e.g., Airbnb agent and Weather agent), with capability matching and tool call execution.

The post concludes with Cybage's service offerings for A2A implementation across financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and retail/e-commerce industries, including proof of concept development, production implementation, training, and ongoing support.

# Google Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol Explained — with Real Working Examples

![Shamim Bhuiyan](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/0*gDbbhT13ylqASHVy.jpg)

3

There are already tons of blog posts and vlogs floating around about agent-based systems, protocols, and AI orchestration. Most of them go deep into the theory or stick to flashy diagrams — but leave developers wondering:*”Okay, but how do I actually use this?”*

In this post, I’ll take a different approach.

Instead of just talking about what the [**Google A2A Protocol**](https://github.com/google/A2A) is, I’ll walk you through how to build a real system with it — **step by step** — using working Python examples. You’ll see how agents can talk to each other, how they collaborate to solve a task like travel planning, and how you can plug this into a local LLM like **Ollama**.

## What Is A2A?

Google’s **Agent-to-Agent (A2A)** protocol is an open specification that allows AI agents to:

Think of it like giving each agent its own little resume, email address, and inbox — so that other agents can contact it and ask for help.

If you’re curious how the protocol works under the hood, please refer to the official protocol [specification](https://google.github.io/A2A/#/) and the excellent hands-on tutorial from the Google Cloud community: [Getting Started with Google A2A — A Hands-On Tutorial](/google-cloud/getting-started-with-google-a2a-a-hands-on-tutorial-for-the-agent2agent-protocol-3d3b5e055127)

However, the official GitHub repository provides good examples to get started, **but for Python beginners, it’s not so straightforward to dive into right away**. That’s why this blog post focuses on a **human-friendly, practical approach** — showing you exactly what to write and how it works, one line at a time.

While Google provides a solid GitHub repository with protocol definitions and usage examples, the experience can be overwhelming for beginners, especially if you’re not comfortable setting up everything from scratch.

**Therefore, I explored several third-party community implementations** that help reduce boilerplate code and offer a much smoother entry point into working with A2A agents. These tools allow you to focus more on logic and behavior rather than wiring up the protocol manually.

On GitHub, I found **two popular high-level Python libraries** that stand out:

`python-a2a`
`a2a-server`

These libraries are great for getting your hands dirty quickly, especially if you’re building practical use cases like agent orchestration or work-flow. And that’s exactly what we’ll use in the upcoming examples.

From these, `python-a2a` **appears to be the more advanced option**. It requires **minimal external dependencies**, making it easier to use in lightweight setups or small projects. With `python-a2a`, you can spin up agents and connect them with just a few lines of code — perfect for quick experimentation or educational use cases.

`python-a2a`
`python-a2a`

## A Simple Overview of How A2A Works

Before we jump into coding, let’s first understand in plain language what the Google Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol is all about. Think of it as a set of rules that let AI agents talk to each other smoothly over the web.

Here are the main building blocks you need to know:

## Agent Card

Every agent has a public “business card” — a small file (usually found at `/.well-known/agent.json`) that tells the world:

`/.well-known/agent.json`

Clients read this card to discover and connect to agents.

## A2A Server

This is the agent that *listens* for requests. It exposes an HTTP API following the A2A protocol. You can think of it like a smart bot that’s ready to accept tasks and do something useful — like fetching weather, searching the web, or generating text.

## A2A Client

This is any app (or another agent) that *sends* tasks to the A2A server. It knows how to talk to the agent using the protocol, and it’s the one that says: “Hey agent, I need you to do this for me.”

## Task

A task is the actual “job” or “command” you want the agent to perform. It could be anything — “What’s the weather in Paris?” or “Summarize this article.” Each task has a unique ID and goes through stages like:

`submitted`
`working`
`input-required`
`completed`
`failed`
`canceled`

## Message

Messages are the back-and-forth communication between the client and the agent during a task. Each message has a role:

`"user"`
`"agent"`

Messages carry actual content (called “Parts”) — like text, images, or structured data — that help the agent understand what to do.

In summary, the A2A protocol just defines a clear way for two smart AI Agents to collaborate over HTTP — one asks for something, the other does it, and they keep track of their conversation along the way.

## Good and Bad parts of the A2A Protocol

While the A2A Protocol provides several strengths that make it well-suited for building agent-based systems, it also comes with certain drawbacks.

### Good Parts of the A2A Protocol

### Bad Parts of the A2A Protocol

## A2A vs. MCP — Not a Battle, but a Partnership

One more thing to clarify: **there’s no competition between A2A and the MCP (Model Context Protocol)**. They serve different but complementary purposes:

In real-world AI applications, **you often need both**:

In the next section, we’ll walk through building a real-world example: a Travel Planner AI that uses multiple A2A agents to provide a personalized itinerary.

## Let’s Build: A Travel Planner AI Agent Using A2A Protocol

To put everything we’ve learned into action, let’s walk through a hands-on example of how to build a **Travel Planner AI** using the A2A protocol.

## Use Case

We’re planning a short holiday trip. We want an AI assistant (an A2A agent server) that can help us decide **where to go and what to do** based on the weather.

Here’s the idea:

By combining these two sources, the travel planner can give smart, personalized suggestions for your trip.

![]()

args.summary:
This article by Shamim Bhuiyan provides a practical, hands-on guide to Google's Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol, an open specification that allows AI agents to communicate and collaborate over HTTP. The author explains the core components of A2A: Agent Card (a business card file at /.well-known/agent.json), A2A Server (listens for requests), A2A Client (sends tasks), Tasks (jobs with unique IDs going through stages like submitted, working, completed, failed), and Messages (back-and-forth communication with role and content parts).

The article highlights that A2A and MCP (Model Context Protocol) are complementary—MCP connects AI agents to external tools/data, while A2A enables agents to communicate with each other directly.

The main focus is a step-by-step tutorial building a Travel Planner AI system using the python-a2a library. The tutorial includes creating four agents: a WeatherAgent (using OpenWeatherMap API on port 8001), a BraveSearchAgent (using Brave Search API on port 8002), a Local LLM Agent (using Ollama with LLaMA 3.2 on port 5001), and a Travel Planner Agent (coordinator using AgentNetwork and A2AClient). These agents collaborate to suggest travel destinations based on weather and local activities, then generate a personalized itinerary using a local LLM.

The author notes that while Google provides official A2A examples, the python-a2a library offers a more beginner-friendly approach with minimal external dependencies. All code is available at github.com/srecon/python-a2a.

The Agent Card Schema Reference is a JSON document specification for the AgentVault ecosystem, serving as a machine-readable "passport" for autonomous agents following the A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol. It enables automatic discovery, authentication, and interaction between agents.

**Core Fields (Required):** schemaVersion, humanReadableId, agentVersion, name, description, url (HTTPS required), provider object, capabilities object, authSchemes array (at least one).

**Optional Fields:** skills, tags, privacyPolicyUrl, termsOfServiceUrl, iconUrl, lastUpdated (ISO 8601).

**Key Objects:**
- **Provider:** name (required), url, support_contact
- **Capabilities:** a2aVersion (required), mcpVersion, supportedMessageParts, supportsPushNotifications, teeDetails
- **TEE Details:** type (required), attestationEndpoint, publicKey, description
- **Authentication Schemes:** scheme (apiKey, oauth2, bearer, or none), tokenUrl (required for oauth2), scopes, service_identifier
- **Skill:** id, name, description (all required), input_schema, output_schema (JSON Schema)

**Authentication Methods:** API Key (Authorization: ApiKey key-value), OAuth2 Client Credentials, Bearer Token (Authorization: Bearer token), or No Authentication.

**Validation Rules:** URL must use HTTPS, authSchemes must contain at least one entry, tokenUrl required for OAuth2, lastUpdated must be valid ISO 8601.

**Best Practices:** Update agentVersion for breaking changes, define input_schema/output_schema for skills, keep lastUpdated current.

**Common Patterns:** Public Agent (no auth), Enterprise Agent (multiple auth options), Secure Agent (TEE-enabled).

# Agent Card Schema Reference[¶](#agent-card-schema-reference "Anchor link to this section")

The Agent Card is a JSON document that describes an A2A-compliant agent. This reference covers the complete JSON Schema specification.

---

## Overview[¶](#overview "Anchor link to this section")

An Agent Card is a JSON document that can be hosted at any URL. Common patterns include:

* **Direct URL**: `https://my-agent.example.com/agent-card.json`
* **Well-known (for discovery)**: `https://domain.com/.well-known/agent-card.json`
* **API path**: `https://api.example.com/agents/weather/agent-card.json`

The `/.well-known/` path is recommended for public agent discovery but is not required.

An Agent Card contains:

* **Identity**: Agent name, description, and provider
* **Capabilities**: Skills and supported protocols
* **Endpoints**: URLs for agent communication
* **Authentication**: Supported auth methods
* **Security**: Cryptographic signatures and trust badges

---

## Minimal Example[¶](#minimal-example "Anchor link to this section")

```
{ { "name": "My Agent",  "name":  "My Agent", "description": "A helpful AI assistant",  "description":  "A helpful AI assistant", "url": "https://my-agent.example.com",  "url":  "https://my-agent.example.com", "version": "1.0.0",  "version":  "1.0.0", "capabilities": {  "capabilities":  { "streaming": false,  "streaming":  false, "pushNotifications": false  "pushNotifications":  false },  }, "skills": [  "skills":  [ {  { "id": "general-chat",  "id":  "general-chat", "name": "General Chat",  "name":  "General Chat", "description": "General conversation and Q&A"  "description":  "General conversation and Q&A" }  } ],  ], "defaultInputModes": ["text"],  "defaultInputModes":  ["text"], "defaultOutputModes": ["text"]  "defaultOutputModes":  ["text"]} }
```

---

## Complete Schema[¶](#complete-schema "Anchor link to this section")

### Root Object[¶](#root-object "Anchor link to this section")

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `string` | ✓ | Human-readable agent name |
| `description` | `string` | ✓ | Brief description of the agent |
| `url` | `string` | ✓ | Base URL of the agent |
| `version` | `string` | ✓ | Agent version (semver recommended) |
| `capabilities` | `object` | ✓ | Agent capabilities |
| `skills` | `array` | ✓ | List of agent skills |
| `defaultInputModes` | `array` | ✓ | Default input modes |
| `defaultOutputModes` | `array` | ✓ | Default output modes |
| `provider` | `object` | Provider information |
| `documentationUrl` | `string` | URL to documentation |
| `authentication` | `object` | Authentication configuration |
| `supportsAuthenticatedExtendedCard` | `boolean` | Extended card support |

### capabilities[¶](#capabilities "Anchor link to this section")

| Field | Type | Required | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `streaming` | `boolean` | ✓ | Supports streaming responses |
| `pushNotifications` | `boolean` | ✓ | Supports push notifications |
| `stateTransitionHistory` | `boolean` | `false` | Tracks state history |

```
{ { "capabilities": {  "capabilities":  { "streaming": true,  "streaming":  true, "pushNotifications": false,  "pushNotifications":  false, "stateTransitionHistory": true  "stateTransitionHistory":  true }  }} }
```

### skills[¶](#skills "Anchor link to this section")

Array of skill objects. At least one skill is required.

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | `string` | ✓ | Unique skill identifier |
| `name` | `string` | ✓ | Human-readable skill name |
| `description` | `string` | ✓ | Skill description |
| `tags` | `array` | Categorization tags |
| `examples` | `array` | Example inputs |
| `inputModes` | `array` | Override default input modes |
| `outputModes` | `array` | Override default output modes |

```

```

### provider[¶](#provider "Anchor link to this section")

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `organization` | `string` | ✓ | Organization name |
| `url` | `string` | Organization website |
| `contactEmail` | `string` | Support email |

```
{ { "provider": {  "provider":  { "organization": "Acme AI",  "organization":  "Acme AI", "url": "https://acme.ai",  "url":  "https://acme.ai", "contactEmail": "[email protected]"  "contactEmail":  "[email protected]" }  }} }
```

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `schemes` | `array` | ✓ | Supported auth schemes |

**Supported schemes:**

| Scheme | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `none` | No authentication required |
| `bearer` | Bearer token authentication |

## Signed Agent Card[¶](#signed-agent-card "Anchor link to this section")

For production deployments, Agent Cards should be signed using JWS (JSON Web Signature).

### Structure[¶](#structure "Anchor link to this section")

A signed Agent Card wraps the card in a JWS envelope:

```
{ { "payload": "",  "payload":  "", "protected": "",  "protected":  "", "signature": ""  "signature":  ""} }
```

### Header[¶](#header "Anchor link to this section")

```
{ { "alg": "EdDSA",  "alg":  "EdDSA", "kid": "did:capiscio:agent:my-agent#key-1"  "kid":  "did:capiscio:agent:my-agent#key-1"} }
```

### Signing Example[¶](#signing-example "Anchor link to this section")

```
 # Generate keys # Generate keyscapiscio key gen --out-priv private.jwk --out-pub public.jwk        # Sign the agent card (coming soon) # Sign the agent card (coming soon)capiscio sign ./agent-card.json --key private.jwk --out signed-agent-card.json       
```

## Extended Card[¶](#extended-card "Anchor link to this section")

An extended card provides additional information available only to authenticated clients.

```
{ { "name": "My Agent",  "name":  "My Agent", "description": "A helpful AI assistant",  "description":  "A helpful AI assistant", "supportsAuthenticatedExtendedCard": true,  "supportsAuthenticatedExtendedCard":  true, "extendedCard": {  "extendedCard":  { "url": "https://my-agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-extended.json",  "url":  "https://my-agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-extended.json", "authentication": {  "authentication":  { "schemes": ["bearer"]  "schemes":  ["bearer"] }  } }  }} }
```

## Validation Rules[¶](#validation-rules "Anchor link to this section")

### Required Fields[¶](#required-fields "Anchor link to this section")

The following fields must be present:

* `name` - Non-empty string
* `description` - Non-empty string
* `url` - Valid HTTPS URL
* `version` - Non-empty string
* `capabilities.streaming` - Boolean
* `capabilities.pushNotifications` - Boolean
* `skills` - Non-empty array
* `skills[].id` - Unique non-empty string
* `skills[].name` - Non-empty string
* `skills[].description` - Non-empty string
* `defaultInputModes` - Non-empty array
* `defaultOutputModes` - Non-empty array

### URL Requirements[¶](#url-requirements "Anchor link to this section")

* Must use HTTPS in production
* Must be publicly accessible (or accessible from validator)
* Should respond within timeout (default 10s)

### Skill Requirements[¶](#skill-requirements "Anchor link to this section")

* Each skill must have a unique `id`
* At least one skill is required
* Skill `id` should be kebab-case (`code-review`, not `CodeReview`)

---

## Best Practices[¶](#best-practices "Anchor link to this section")

### Naming[¶](#naming "Anchor link to this section")

* Use clear, descriptive names
* Avoid generic names like "Agent" or "Assistant"
* Include your organization name if appropriate

### Descriptions[¶](#descriptions "Anchor link to this section")

* Write clear, concise descriptions
* Explain what the agent does, not how
* Include key capabilities

### Skills[¶](#skills_1 "Anchor link to this section")

* Define focused, single-purpose skills
* Use descriptive skill names
* Provide helpful examples
* Use appropriate tags for discovery

### Versioning[¶](#versioning "Anchor link to this section")

* Use semantic versioning (semver)
* Update version when capabilities change
* Document breaking changes

args.summary:
The Agent Card Schema Reference defines the JSON specification for describing an A2A-compliant agent. An Agent Card is a JSON document that can be hosted at any URL, with recommended patterns including direct URLs, well-known paths (/.well-known/agent-card.json) for discovery, or API paths. The card contains identity information (name, description, provider), capabilities (skills and supported protocols), endpoints for agent communication, authentication methods, and security features like cryptographic signatures.

Required fields include: name, description, url (HTTPS), version, capabilities (streaming and pushNotifications booleans), skills (non-empty array with unique IDs), defaultInputModes, and defaultOutputModes. Skills can include tags, examples, and mode overrides. The capabilities object supports streaming, pushNotifications, and optionally stateTransitionHistory.

The schema supports authentication schemes: none, bearer, oauth2, and apiKey. Input/output modes include text, file, image, audio, video, and structured JSON data. For production, Agent Cards should be signed using JWS (JSON Web Signature) with EdDSA algorithm. Extended cards provide additional information for authenticated clients. Validation rules require HTTPS URLs, unique kebab-case skill IDs, and at least one skill. Best practices include using semantic versioning, focused single-purpose skills, and clear descriptive names.
